Good morning. This is the status of the five actions from the board meeting, in order. Item one, the Houston budget: closed. The board signed off on it on Thursday and there is nothing outstanding. Item two, the supplier quote: late. Procurement is carrying a three-week backlog after the holiday, so nobody has refused anything, the request is simply sitting in a queue. I will chase it up this afternoon. Item three, the contract review: this is the real bottleneck. Legal has not moved for two weeks and everything else is waiting on that signature. If it has not moved by Friday I am going to escalate it to the board. Item four, the Houston site visit: booked. I am meeting the local team at nine on Thursday the fourteenth. And item five, the insurance renewal, which has not started. We are going to loop in counsel before we reply to the broker, and finance and I are touching base on Wednesday. Two items outstanding, one bottleneck, no surprises.

I want to say something about the sentence I will look into it, because it is the most expensive sentence in corporate English. It has no owner and it has no date. The person who writes it thinks they have promised something. The person who reads it does not know whether it is a decision, an intention, or a very polite no. So in every action item I write, there are three things and never fewer: a verb, an owner and a date. And the tense does real work there. If I decided it on the call, while I was speaking, I write will. I will chase it up this afternoon. If the plan already existed before I opened my mouth, I write going to. We are going to loop in counsel, as we agreed on Monday. And if the thing is already arranged, with a person and a time in the diary, I use the present continuous. I am meeting counsel at nine on Thursday. One last habit, and it is the one that keeps relationships. Before I escalate anything, I nudge once, I chase up once, and I tell the owner the exact date on which I am going to escalate. Nobody has ever been angry with me for escalating. They get angry when it is a surprise.

First, you write the action item properly: a verb, an owner and a date, so nobody can read it two ways. Then, a few days later, you send a friendly nudge to the owner, because most things are simply sitting in a queue. After that, if nothing arrives, you chase it up and you find out what the real bottleneck is. Next, you warn the owner: you say the exact date on which you are going to escalate, so that nothing is a surprise. Finally, if the date passes, you escalate to the person above, you loop in whoever needs to see it, and you update the tracker so the board reads the same story you do.
